4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_intro: Connect total benefit, total cost, marginal benefit, marginal cost and net benefit across four linked panels.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.card_prompt: Move the quantity q and explain why net benefit rises before MB = MC and falls afterwards.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.intro_html: This graph presents the same choice in four equivalent ways. The top panels show total and marginal benefit and cost; the bottom panels show net benefit and the marginal change in net benefit. Move \(q\) and follow the same quantity across all four panels.
4-axis-Cost-Benefit.full_html:
What the four panels show

Suppose an agent chooses a quantity \(q\). Total benefit is \(B(q)\), total cost is \(C(q)\), and net benefit is

\[NB(q)=B(q)-C(q).\]

  • Top left: total benefit and total cost. At the selected quantity, their vertical difference is net benefit.
  • Top right: marginal benefit and marginal cost. These measure the benefit and cost of a small increase in quantity.
  • Bottom left: net benefit as a function of quantity.
  • Bottom right: marginal net benefit, which is the slope of the net-benefit curve.

Why the optimum occurs at MB = MC

Differentiating net benefit gives

\[NB'(q)=B'(q)-C'(q)=MB(q)-MC(q).\]

If \(MB(q)>MC(q)\), increasing quantity adds more benefit than cost, so net benefit rises. If \(MB(q)<MC(q)\), the next unit adds more cost than benefit, so net benefit falls. At an interior maximum, the slope of net benefit is zero:

The equality is not a separate rule imposed on the model. It is another way of saying that the net-benefit curve has reached a stationary point.

A worked observation from the default graph

The default functions are \(B(q)=0.7q\) and \(C(q)=0.1q^2\). Therefore \(MB=0.7\) and \(MC=0.2q\). Setting them equal gives \(q^*=3.5\). At that quantity,

\[NB(3.5)=0.7(3.5)-0.1(3.5)^2=1.225.\]

Move \(q\) slightly below and above 3.5. Below it, marginal net benefit is positive and the net-benefit curve slopes upward. Above it, marginal net benefit is negative and the curve slopes downward.

Check your model

Do not confuse total and marginal objects. The height of \(B(q)\) is total benefit, while the slope of that curve is marginal benefit. Similarly, the gap \(B(q)-C(q)\) is net benefit, while the gap \(MB(q)-MC(q)\) is marginal net benefit.

Explore further: when is MB = MC not enough?

The condition \(MB=MC\) identifies a stationary point, not automatically a global maximum. With irregular functions there may be several intersections, or the best choice may be at a boundary. In the default graph, the net-benefit function is concave, so the intersection identifies the unique maximum.

Try increasing the fixed-cost parameter \(a_C\). This shifts total cost upward and net benefit downward, but it does not change marginal cost. The maximizing quantity therefore stays the same even though the maximum level of net benefit falls.

Elasticity-Flexible-Demand.full_html:
Elasticity of demand is computed using the point elasticity formula:\[E_d = \frac{dQ}{dP} \cdot \frac{P}{Q}\]

Notice that elasticity of demand remains constant at all price level, it is because the Demand curve is a power function. In the example, \(E_d = -2\), meaning quantity demanded changes by 2% for every 1% increase in price.

Elasticity-Staircase-Demand.full_html:
This graph shows a staircase (step) demand curve, where quantity changes only at discrete price levels. Because the curve is piecewise vertical and horizontal, elasticity behaves very differently from smooth demand curves.

Vertical segments:

When the curve is vertical except at \(Q = 0\), quantity does not react to price changes, thus, the elasticity of demand is 0.

Horizontal segments:

On horizontal steps, price does not change (\( dP = 0 \)), the percentage change in price is zero, so demand elasticity is undefined.

Lectorial.card_intro: Construct benefit, cost and net-benefit curves, then locate the optimal choice using both the graph and MB = MC.
Lectorial.card_prompt: Graph the three functions, estimate the maximizing value of H, and then verify it algebraically.
Lectorial.intro_html:
Suppose the total benefit and total cost from choosing \\(H\\) are

\\[B(H)=654H-40H^2,\\qquad C(H)=110H+40H^2,\\qquad H\\geq 0.\\]

  1. Define net benefit, \\(N_B(H)\\), and use its graph to estimate the value of \\(H\\) that maximises net benefit.
  2. Now calculate marginal benefit and marginal cost. Check whether your proposed optimum satisfies \\(M_B(H)=M_C(H)\\).
  3. Explain why net benefit rises when \\(M_B(H)>M_C(H)\\) and falls when \\(M_B(H)<M_C(H)\\). How does this explain the shape of the net-benefit curve?
  4. Would solving \\(B(H)=C(H)\\) identify the net-benefit-maximising choice? Explain why or why not.

Enter your proposed value using the \\(H_{opt}\\) slider. The graph will mark the point only when your answer is sufficiently close.

"
Lectorial.answer_html:
The task

The graph defines

\[B(H)=654H-40H^2,\qquad C(H)=110H+40H^2.\]

  1. Graph \(B(H)\) and \(C(H)\).
  2. Define and graph \(NB(H)=B(H)-C(H)\).
  3. Use the graph to estimate the value of \(H\) that maximizes net benefit.
  4. Differentiate the benefit and cost functions and check the condition \(MB(H)=MC(H)\).
  5. Enter your proposed value as \(H_{opt}\). The red cross appears when the marginal condition is satisfied within the stated tolerance.

What you should notice before calculating

Benefit is hump-shaped because its marginal benefit eventually becomes negative. Cost is increasing and convex. Net benefit is therefore also a downward-opening quadratic. The maximizing value of \(H\) is at the top of the net-benefit curve—not where benefit is highest, and not where total benefit equals total cost.

Use the graph first. It should tell you approximately where the answer lies and whether your algebra is plausible.

Show the algebraic solution

Net benefit is

\[NB(H)=544H-80H^2.\]

The marginal functions are

\[MB(H)=654-80H,\qquad MC(H)=110+80H.\]

At the interior optimum,

\[654-80H=110+80H,\]

so \(H^*=3.4\). Substituting this into net benefit gives \(NB(3.4)=924.8\).

Check your reasoning

Why not choose a slightly larger value of \(H\)? Immediately to the right of 3.4, marginal cost exceeds marginal benefit, so the additional cost is larger than the additional benefit and net benefit falls. Immediately to the left, marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost, so a small increase in \(H\) raises net benefit.

For teaching and test construction

The same structure can generate a new exercise by replacing the definitions of \(B(H)\) and \(C(H)\). Keep the marginal expressions and answer marker hidden while students work. Before using a new version, check that the proposed domain contains the optimum and that the tolerance allows sensible decimal approximations.

Utility-Max.card_intro: View indifference curves as level curves of a utility surface and see utility maximisation as the highest feasible point on that surface.
Utility-Max.card_prompt: Move a bundle along the budget line and compare its 2D indifference curve with its height on the 3D utility surface.
Utility-Max.intro_html: This optional graph connects the familiar two-dimensional consumer-choice diagram to the three-dimensional utility surface behind it. A bundle \((x,y)\) lies on the floor; its height \(z=u(x,y)\) records its utility ranking.
Utility-Max.full_html:
From bundles to a utility surface

The horizontal axes measure quantities of goods \(x\) and \(y\). The vertical axis records

\[z=u(x,y)=x^ay^b.\]

Every bundle on the \((x,y)\) plane maps to one point on the surface. Moving upward means moving to a bundle assigned a higher utility number.

An indifference curve is obtained by fixing utility at some level \(\bar u\):

\[u(x,y)=\bar u.\]

In three dimensions, this is the intersection between the utility surface and a horizontal plane at height \(\bar u\). Project that intersection down onto the \((x,y)\) plane and you obtain the ordinary two-dimensional indifference curve.

How to explore the graph

  1. Rotate the graph so that you can see both the floor and the utility surface.
  2. Turn on Plotting (x,y,u(x,y)). Change \(x_2\) and \(y_2\) and follow the vertical segment from the bundle to the surface.
  3. Turn on Indifference Curve. Notice that the 2D curve on the floor and the corresponding curve on the surface represent the same utility level.
  4. Turn on Moving along indifference curve. As the quantities change along that curve, the point moves horizontally across the surface but its height remains fixed.
  5. Turn on the budget-line folders. Change \(x_1\) and observe the utility obtained by each feasible bundle.

Utility maximisation on the surface

The budget constraint is

\[p_xx+p_yy\le I.\]

On the floor, this determines the feasible set. The boundary can be written as \(y=I/p_y-(p_x/p_y)x\). When the budget line is lifted onto the utility surface, it becomes the curve

\[z=u\!\left(x,\frac{I}{p_y}-\frac{p_x}{p_y}x\right).\]

The consumer's problem is to find the highest point on this feasible curve. Viewed from above, that same point is where the highest attainable indifference curve is tangent to the budget line.

A worked observation from the default graph

The default graph has \(a=b=1\), \(p_x=p_y=5\), and \(I=15\). Thus \(u(x,y)=xy\) and the budget line is \(x+y=3\). Along the budget line,

\[u(x,3-x)=x(3-x).\]

This is maximized at \(x^*=1.5\), so \(y^*=1.5\) and \(u^*=2.25\). At that bundle,

\[MRS_{xy}=\frac{MU_x}{MU_y}=\frac{y}{x}=1=\frac{p_x}{p_y}.\]

For example, the graph initially places one budget-line point near \((1.08,1.92)\). Its utility is about 2.07, below the maximum. Move toward \((1.5,1.5)\) and the point climbs the feasible curve; move past it and the point descends.

Check your model

Do not interpret the vertical distance between two points as a measurable difference in happiness. Utility is ordinal: it ranks bundles. A strictly increasing transformation can change the numerical height and shape of the surface while preserving the same indifference curves and the same choices.

Also, utility does not rise as you move toward the “optimal point” along one indifference curve. Utility is constant everywhere on a given indifference curve. The optimum lies on the highest indifference curve the budget allows the consumer to reach.

Explore further: why the 2D graph is usually enough

The three-dimensional surface is useful for seeing where indifference curves come from, but consumer choice depends only on the ranking of feasible bundles. A contour map preserves that ranking while being easier to draw and compare with a budget line. This is why the course usually works with two-dimensional indifference curves.

The tangency condition applies to the smooth interior solution shown here. With perfect substitutes, perfect complements or a binding boundary, the optimum may be a corner or kink and must be checked directly.

IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_intro: Decompose the effect of a tax on good 2 into a relative-price substitution effect and a purchasing-power income effect.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.card_prompt: Increase the tax, construct the compensated budget line, and compare the old, compensated and final bundles.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.intro_html: A price change does two things at once: it changes relative prices and it changes purchasing power. This graph separates those mechanisms for Cobb–Douglas utility by comparing the original optimum, a utility-compensated optimum at the new prices, and the final uncompensated optimum.
IE-SE-CobbDouglas.full_html:
Start with the three budget lines

The consumer has utility \(u(x,y)=xy\) and begins with prices \(p_1,p_2\) and income \(I\). A tax \(t\) on good 2 changes its price from \(p_2\) to \(p_2+t\).

  • Original budget line: \(p_1x+p_2y=I\).
  • New budget line: \(p_1x+(p_2+t)y=I\).
  • Compensated budget line: parallel to the new budget line, but shifted outward until it is tangent to the original indifference curve.

The tax raises the price of good 2, so the budget line pivots inward around the good-1 intercept. The compensated line is imaginary: it asks what the consumer would choose at the new relative prices if enough income were provided to restore the original utility level.

The decomposition

Let the original bundle be \((x_0,y_0)\), the compensated bundle be \((x_c,y_c)\), and the final bundle be \((x_1,y_1)\).

  • Substitution effect: the move from the original bundle to the compensated bundle. Utility is held at its original level, so the movement is caused by the change in relative prices.
  • Income effect: the move from the compensated bundle to the final bundle. Relative prices are now fixed, so the movement is caused by the reduction in purchasing power.
  • Total effect: the move from the original bundle to the final bundle.

\[\text{Total effect}=\text{Substitution effect}+\text{Income effect}.\]

A positive effect means that the quantity of the relevant good rises; a negative effect means that it falls. The sign does not mean “moves opposite to price” by definition.

How to use this graph

  1. Turn on the original budget line and original optimum.
  2. Turn on the tax budget line and the new optimum.
  3. Turn on the compensating-variation folder and the arrow decomposition.
  4. Increase \(t_{ax}\) and track the three optimal bundles.

The graph also contains a manually adjustable transfer \(S\). If you use the manual decomposition folders, set \(S=S_c\); otherwise the intermediate line will not hold utility constant and the displayed “substitution effect” will not be a compensated substitution effect.

A worked observation from the default graph

With \(p_1=6\), \(p_2=1\), \(I=174\), and \(t=1.1\), Cobb–Douglas demand is

\[x=\frac{I}{2p_1},\qquad y=\frac{I}{2p_2}.\]

The original bundle is \((14.5,87)\). After the tax, the uncompensated bundle is approximately \((14.5,41.43)\). The compensated bundle is approximately \((21.01,60.04)\).

For good 2, both effects are negative: it becomes relatively more expensive, and the loss of purchasing power further lowers its consumption. For good 1, the substitution effect is positive but the income effect is negative. With this equal-share Cobb–Douglas utility, those two effects cancel exactly, so the final quantity of good 1 returns to 14.5.

Check your model

Compensation restores the consumer's utility; it does not restore the old bundle. At the new relative prices the old bundle is generally not what the consumer wants. This is why a compensating rebate need not undo the consumption effect of a per-unit tax.

Explore further: what is special about this Cobb–Douglas example?

The unchanged uncompensated demand for good 1 is not a general property of convex preferences. It occurs here because \(u(x,y)=xy\) allocates one-half of income to each good, and neither \(I\) nor \(p_1\) changes. With another utility function, a tax on good 2 can change the final demand for good 1.

If the same proportional sales tax were placed on both goods, the market exchange rate would be unchanged. There would then be no substitution effect from the tax itself—only a purchasing-power effect.
